The first tournament where Russia could return is the men's world junior championship in Edmonton and Red Deer, Canada, starting on December 26 [File: Alexander Fedorov/Reuters]By APPublished On 30 Oct 202630 Oct 2026
Russia must be allowed to return to the ice hockey world championships, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled, overturning an exclusion in place since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The ruling is a major win for Russia against efforts to bar it from international sport due to the war in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin is a noted hockey fan who has previously played exhibition games with former stars.

CAS overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions that excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season, including the men’s and women’s world championships. Russia also missed the Olympic tournaments this year.
Russia’s return throws into uncertainty how the men’s world championship will work next year in Germany, given that Ukraine has also qualified.
CAS ruling cites lack of evidence on security over Russia
In a brief statement, CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support the IIHF’s security concerns.
CAS said its ruling did not address issues such as whether Russia should be required to play without national symbols as a team of neutral athletes, as in some other Olympic sports, or other “organisational consequences”.

[Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters]By Nils AdlerPublished On 30 Oct 202630 Oct 2026
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, says hackers have stolen about $6.3bn in what appears to have been the biggest crypto heist on record.
The company, which was co-founded by the Chinese-born Canadian billionaire Changpeng Zhao, suspended deposits and withdrawals on Thursday and said it would cover all losses, telling Al Jazeera in a statement that user funds were “safe”.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Global stock markets rise as investors continue to bet on AIlist 2 of 4North Korea fires missiles as row over landmine blast intensifieslist 3 of 4North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report sayslist 4 of 4Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in historyend of list
Two United States blockchain analysis firms have claimed the attack originated in North Korea.
So how did it happen, and what does it mean for the crypto market? Here’s what you need to know:
What happened?
Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis say most of the theft unfolded over about 20 minutes, starting late on Thursday.
“An attacker moved approximately 6.36 billion USD out of Binance wallets on 10 blockchains,” TRM reported.
That dwarfs the previous record of $1.5bn, which was stolen from the exchange Bybit in February 2025.
Binance said about $3bn of that has since been frozen, including more than $2.3bn by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle, according to the Reuters news agency.
Binance has not stated what has happened to the remaining $3.3bn.

A few minutes past 9am on Wednesday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez posted a message on X declaring there were “lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country”.
His left-wing Socialist Party (PSOE) had sought to seize upon anger over Spain’s housing crisis as a campaign issue ahead of the November 29 election.

Less than an hour later, news of a deadly train crash began to emerge, transforming the campaign. The safety of Spain’s railways, its infrastructure and the government’s ability to deliver essential public services are now key issues after 69 people were killed nine months after a similar disaster.
The mood has changed and Sanchez’s Socialists could be in trouble, analysts say, as the conservative opposition has been handed new grounds to challenge the government on competence and security.
“There are no winners in this tragedy, but it marks a new tone for the campaign where the conservative party could be more comfortable,” said Yolanda Roman, global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, referring to the Popular Party (PP) that has been leading in the polls.

Georgia is among a number of key “swing” or “battleground” states being fought for hardest in the run-up to the United States midterm elections next week.
The southern state has been so competitive in recent federal election cycles that its three most recent Senate matchups went to runoffs.

Both the Republican and the Democratic parties have spent considerable time and resources trying to win the state during the closing stretch of their campaigns.
US President Donald Trump and former US President Barack Obama both held rallies in Georgia this week, as the parties present their closing messages ahead of next week’s vote.
Why is Georgia such a key state for the midterms?
Georgia is a major focus for Trump, and he has campaigned twice in Dalton, Georgia, in the past two weeks.
The state is a source of personal grievance for the president, primarily because it was where he disputed his preelection loss in 2020.
Trump refused to concede to Joe Biden following his defeat but failed to overturn the results in several states, including Georgia.
In January, Trump urged a Georgia official to recalculate the state’s presidential election results in his favour. Trump said “I just want to find 11,780 votes, which is one more than we have”.

Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta has been branded a 'foreign agent' by Moscow (File: Reuters)By Al Jazeera Staff and AFPPublished On 30 Oct 202630 Oct 2026
Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, citing pressure from the authorities.
The independent outlet’s editorial board said in a statement released on Friday that the newspaper has been forced to end its operations.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4North Koreans being recruited into forced labour in Russia, report sayslist 2 of 4Why is Russia sending fighter jets and air defences to Ethiopia?list 3 of 4At least 14 people killed in attack on Ukraine train stationlist 4 of 4Russian oil refinery struck as Ukraine renews drone attacksend of list
The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. The authorities recently searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s senior editor and arrested the editor-in-chief.
“The newspaper is gone. The Russian authorities and … intelligence services forced the editorial staff to cease operations,” the editorial board said in the statement, which was entitled: “We were killed.”
Viewed as a relative bastion of independent journalism in Russia, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement published on YouTube. “On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
Earlier this month, Sokolov was taken in for questioning as Russian authorities searched his home due, they said, to a link to a criminal case involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin.
